The Algebra of Parity Games
Robin Piedeleu

Abstract
In recent work, Watanabe, Eberhart, Asada, and Hasuo have shown that parity games can be seen as string diagrams, that is, as the morphisms of a symmetric monoidal category, an algebraic structure with two different operations of composition. Furthermore, they have shown that the winning regions associated to a given game can be computed functorially, i.e. compositionally. Building on their results, this paper focuses on the equational properties of parity games, giving them a sound and complete axiomatisation. The payoff is that any parity game can be solved using equational reasoning directly at the level of the string diagram that represents it. Finally, we translate the diagrammatic language of parity games to an equally expressive symbolic calculus with fixpoints, and equip it with its own equational theory.



I
Introduction

Parity games are the computational engine that powers a number of important problems in logic, formal verification, and synthesis. For example, solving parity games is equivalent to the model-checking problem for the modal
\mu
-calculus
[
BW18
]
. This makes parity games fundamental to verifying the correctness of complex systems. Similarly, problems like validity and satisfiability in several modal logics can be reduced to parity game solving
[
Wil01
]
.

Famously, the complexity-theoretic status of parity games remains open: it is not known whether they can be solved in polynomial time, though we know the problem belongs to the intersection of the UP and co-UP classes
[
Jur98
]
. This continues to drive extensive research into more efficient algorithms
[
JPZ08
,
CDF+19
]
.

Recently, Watanabe, Eberhart, Asada, and Hasuo have introduced
open
parity games, allowing for a compositional treatment of these games
[
WEAH21
]
. In their work, the labelled graphs associated to open parity games are recast as string diagrams, that is, as the morphisms of a symmetric monoidal category, an algebraic structure with two different operations of composition, sequential and parallel. They generalise the notion of winning regions to open parity games and show that these define a monoidal functor into a suitable semantic category. In other words, they demonstrate that solving (open) parity games can be done compositionally: the solutions of some game can be computed by composing the semantics of its components. This pioneering work opens up the study of parity games using the tools of algebra, in particular equational reasoning, which is the focus of our paper.

Contributions

While in their work, Watanabe et al define a diagrammatic syntax for open parity games, their presentation involves an infinite number of generators, one for each possible node occurring in a parity game. For example, there is one generator for a parity
5
node owned by Player
1
with two inputs and three outputs, one for a similar node with three inputs and one outputs, and so on. The first contribution of this work is to identify a
finite
set of generators from which all open parity games can be constructed,
i.e.
a set which is
universal
for open parity games (Theorem
III.3
).

Our second and more noteworthy contribution is to identify all the algebraic laws that govern the relationship between open parity games: more specifically, we give a finite set of equalities which is
sound and complete
for the chosen semantics (Theorems
IV.1
and
IV.6
). In other words, any two open parity games with the same semantics are provably equal using our equational theory. As a result, it is possible to solve a given parity game using only equational reasoning, going one significant step further than the work of Watanabe et al. In their own words
[
WEAH21
, Remark 3.16]

“an equational characterization of the equivalence of open parity games […] seems challenging, however, given the complexity of solving parity games, and we leave it as future work.”

This is precisely the problem that this paper solves.

Our final contribution is a translation of the diagrammatic presentation of parity games into a standard algebraic syntax with fixpoints. The language and its translation follow the work of Hasegawa
[
Has12
]
. We believe it will be helpful to those who are less familiar with string diagrams and demonstrates the practical value of our work in potential implementations.

The reader might legitimately wonder why we would want an equational axiomatisation when equivalence of parity games (or simply solving them) is decidable. We believe our equational characterisation has independent value, for several reasons.
First and foremost, equational reasoning is compositional: the solution of a complex game can be found from iteratively solving its component games. This is particularly valuable in cases where games have some regularity that allows us to reuse previously computed solutions
[
RSS14
,
Wat24
]
. Relatedly, our algebraic way of reasoning about parity games grounds the solution to each game in
local
reasoning principles (
i.e.
axioms). This can be especially valuable in scenarios where these solutions must be communicated, checked, or automated.
Finally, our diagrammatic axiomatisation links to a growing body of work on related graphical formalisms, in particular to previous work on automata or Boolean satisfiability, where similar algebraic structure appears
[
PZ23a
,
GPZ23
]
.

Outline

We start with few preliminaries on parity games, before introducing
open
parity games and their semantics in Section
II
.
Then, in Section
III
, we introduce the diagrammatic syntax we will use throughout, give its interpretation, and show that it is sufficiently expressive to encode all open parity games (Theorem
III.3
). In Section
IV
, we give the equational theory of open parity games and prove it is sound and complete for the intended semantics (Theorems
IV.1
and
IV.6
). In Section
V
, we consider an equally expressive symbolic syntax. In conclusion, we examine related work and open with a few directions for future research.

Notation

We will write
\left[n\right]
for the ordinal
\{1,\dots,n\}
,
[f,g]\,:\,X+Y\to Z
for the co-pairing of two maps
f\,:\,X\to Z
and
g\,:\,Y\to Z
, and
\mathtt{l}(x),\mathtt{r}(y)
for the two inclusions of
x\in X
and
y\in Y
in the coproduct
X+Y
. We will also write
!_{\emptyset}
for the only map out of the empty set. We denote by
R^{\star}
the transitive closure of a binary relation
R
, and by
V^{*}
the set of words over some set
V
.

II
Background on (open) parity games

We fix a natural number
M\geq 2
and let
\mathbb{P}=\{0,1,\dots,M\}
be our set of
priorities
. All the results in this paper are parametric in this choice of upper bound, which can always be increased in practice to accommodate parity games with arbitrarily large priorities.

II-A

Parity games

Definition II.1
.

A
parity game

\mathcal{G}=(V,V_{0},E,\Omega)
is a tuple consisting of a set of
positions

V
, partitioned into two subsets
V_{0}
and
V_{1}:=V\setminus V_{0}
indicating which position belong to Player
0
or
1
respectively, a set of (directed)
edges

E\subseteq V\times V
, and a labelling function
\Omega\,:\,V\to\mathbb{P}
, assigning a
priority
to each position of the game.

A
play
is a sequence of positions in
V
such that
(v_{n},v_{n+1})\in E
. A finite play is
winning
for Player
0
(resp.
1
) if it ends on a position in
V_{1}
(resp.
V_{0}
). Winning conditions for infinite plays are more interesting and follow what is known as the
parity condition
: an infinite play
(v_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}
is
winning
for Player
0
(resp.
1
), if the maximum priority that occurs infinitely often is even (resp. odd). In other words, Player
0
wins
p
if
\limsup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\Omega(v_{n})
is even, otherwise it is
losing
(
i.e.
winning for Player
1
). A strategy for Player
0
is a function
\sigma\,:\,V^{*}V_{0}\to V
where
(v_{k},\sigma(v_{1}\dots v_{k}))\in E
, that is, it is a function that chooses a new position adjacent to
v_{k}
for each finite sequence of positions
v_{1}\dots v_{k}
ending in a position in
V_{0}
(that Player
0
controls). Strategies for Player
1
are defined in the same way, replacing
0
with
1
in the preceding sentence.

Solving a parity game involves determining, for a given position
v
, which player has a winning strategy for any opponent strategy, starting from
v
. The key result about parity games is that they are
positionally determined
: each position is winning for exactly one of the two players
[
EJ91
]
.

Typically, parity games are represented as a directed graph whose diamond nodes represent positions owned by Player
0
, square nodes represent positions owned by Player
1
, with labels indicating the corresponding priorities.

Example II.2
.

The game
(\{v_{tl},v_{tr},v_{bl},v_{br}\},\{v_{tl},v_{bl}\},E,\Omega)
, where
E=\{(v_{tl},v_{tr}),(v_{tr},v_{tl}),(v_{tl},v_{bl}),(v_{bl},v_{br}),(v_{br},v_{bl})
,
(v_{br},v_{tl}),(v_{br},v_{tr})\}

and
\Omega:v_{tl}\mapsto 4,v_{tr}\mapsto 1,v_{bl}\mapsto 3,v_{br}\mapsto 2
, can be depicted as

2
4
1
3

In this game, the top nodes
\{v_{tl},v_{tr}\}
are winning positions for Player
0
and the bottom ones are winning positions for Player
1
. Indeed, consider the bottom right node
v_{br}
for example: Player
1
can choose to go left to
v_{bl}
, at which point Player
0
has no choice but to come back to the starting position; this defines an infinite play whose highest priority is odd (
viz.

3
), so Player
1
wins. If Player
1
start by going up diagonally to
v_{tl}
node, Player
0
would win by responding with
v_{tr}
node.

II-B

Open parity games and their algebraic operations

We now extend the usual definition of parity games to include incoming and outgoing edges, in order to be able to compose them
[
WEAH21
, Section 2]
.

Definition II.3
.

An
open parity game
is a tuple
\mathcal{A}=(\overline{m},\overline{n},V,V_{0},E,\Omega)
where

•

\overline{m}=(\overrightarrow{m},\overleftarrow{m})
and
\overline{n}=(\overrightarrow{n},\overleftarrow{n})
are pairs of natural numbers, and we call
\mathsf{in}^{\mathcal{A}}:=\left[\overrightarrow{m}+\overleftarrow{n}\right]
the set of
entry positions
and
\mathsf{out}^{\mathcal{A}}=\left[\overleftarrow{m}+\overrightarrow{n}\right]
the set of
exit positions
;

•

V
is a finite set of
internal positions
;

•

V_{0}
indicates the set of internal positions which belong to Player
0
(and
V_{1}:=V\setminus V_{0}
those that belong to Player
1
);

•

E
is a relation
E\subseteq(\mathsf{in}^{\mathcal{A}}+V)\times(V+\mathsf{out}^{\mathcal{A}})
whose elements are called
edges
;

•

there is a unique edge out of each entry position and a unique edge into each exit position;

•

\Omega
is a function
V\to\mathbb{P}
assigning a priority to each internal position.

Finally, we write
\mathcal{A}\,:\,\overline{m}\to\overline{n}
, and call
\overline{m}
its
domain
and
\overline{n}
its
codomain
.

We represent open parity games much like plain parity games, but with entry positions as incoming edges without any source and exit positions as outgoing edges without any target (with the total order on each side read from top to bottom).

Example II.4
.

The following

2
4
1
3

represents the open parity game
((2,0),(2,0)
,
\{v_{tl},v_{tr},v_{bl},v_{br}\}
,
\{v_{tl},v_{bl}\}
,
E,\Omega)
where
E
and
\Omega
are defined as in Example
II.2
.

Definition II.5
.

Let
\mathcal{A}\,:\,\overline{m}\to\overline{n}
and
\mathcal{B}\,:\,\overline{n}\to\overline{o}
be two open parity games. Their
composition

\mathcal{A}\,;\,\mathcal{B}\,:\,\overline{m}\to\overline{o}
is the open parity game
(\overline{m},\overline{o},V^{\mathcal{A}}+V^{\mathcal{B}},V_{0}^{\mathcal{A}}+V_{0}^{\mathcal{B}},E^{\mathcal{A}\,;\,\mathcal{B}},[\Omega^{\mathcal{A}},\Omega^{\mathcal{B}}])
, such that
E^{\mathcal{A}\,;\,\mathcal{B}}:=

E^{\mathcal{A}}\setminus\big((\mathsf{in}^{\mathcal{A}}+V^{\mathcal{A}})\times\mathsf{out}^{\mathcal{A}}\big)+E^{\mathcal{B}}\setminus\big(\mathsf{in}^{\mathcal{B}}\times(V^{\mathcal{B}}+\mathsf{out}^{\mathcal{B}})\big)+E^{\prime}

where

\displaystyle E^{\prime}:=\big\{(v,w)\mid\exists i\,\big((v,\mathtt{r}(i))\in E^{\mathcal{A}}\land(\mathtt{l}(i),w)\in E^{\mathcal{B}}\big)\big\}\cup\quad

\displaystyle\;\big\{(w,v)\mid\exists i\,\big((w,\mathtt{r}(\overrightarrow{o}+i))\in E^{\mathcal{B}}\land(\mathtt{l}(\overrightarrow{m}+i),v)\in E^{\mathcal{A}}\big)\big\}

Note that we abuse notation slightly: we write
E^{\mathcal{A}}\setminus\big((\mathsf{in}^{\mathcal{A}}+V^{\mathcal{A}})\times\mathsf{out}^{\mathcal{A}}\big)
to mean
E^{\mathcal{A}}\setminus\big((\mathsf{in}^{\mathcal{A}}+V^{\mathcal{A}})\times\mathtt{r}^{*}(\mathsf{out}^{\mathcal{A}})\big)
, where
\mathtt{r}^{*}(\mathsf{out}^{\mathcal{A}})
is the image of the right insertion
\mathtt{r}
in the coproduct
V^{\mathcal{A}}+\mathsf{out}^{\mathcal{A}}
.

Intuitively, the composition of two open parity games identifies the right nodes (entries and exits) of the first morphism with the left nodes (entries and exits) of the second and hides them,
i.e.
, replaces them each with an edge in the appropriate direction.

Example II.6
.

The open parity game from Example
II.4
is the composite of the following two games:

4
3
2
1

The example below will be the unit for this operation of composition.

Example II.7
.

We call the game
(\overline{m},\overline{m},\emptyset,\emptyset,\{(i,i)\mid i\in\left[\overrightarrow{m}+\overrightarrow{n}\right]\},!_{\emptyset})
the
identity
over
\overline{m}
and write it as
\mathsf{id}_{\overline{m}}\,:\,\overline{m}\to\overline{m}
.

Definition II.8
.

Let
\mathcal{A}_{1}\,:\,\overline{m}_{1}\to\overline{n}_{1}
and
\mathcal{A}_{2}\,:\,\overline{m}_{2}\to\overline{n}_{2}
be two open parity games. Their
monoidal product

\mathcal{A}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{A}_{2}\,:\,\overline{m}_{1}+\overline{m}_{2}\to\overline{n}_{1}+\overline{n}_{2}
is the open parity game
((\overrightarrow{m}_{1}+\overrightarrow{m}_{2},\overleftarrow{m}_{1}+\overleftarrow{m}_{2}),(\overrightarrow{n}_{1}+\overrightarrow{n}_{2},\overleftarrow{n}_{1}+\overleftarrow{n}_{2}),V^{\mathcal{A}_{1}}+V^{\mathcal{A}_{2}},V_{0}^{\mathcal{A}_{1}}+V_{0}^{\mathcal{A}_{2}},E^{\mathcal{A}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{A}_{2}},[\Omega^{\mathcal{A}_{1}},\Omega^{\mathcal{A}_{2}}])
, with

E^{\mathcal{A}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{A}_{2}}:=E^{\mathcal{A}_{1}}+E^{\mathcal{A}_{2}}_{\downarrow}

where
E^{\mathcal{A}_{2}}_{\downarrow}
shifts entry and exit positions of
E^{\mathcal{A}_{2}}
by
\overrightarrow{m}_{1}+\overleftarrow{n}_{1}
and
\overleftarrow{m}_{1}+\overrightarrow{n}_{1}
respectively: more precisely, it is the relation defined by
(v,v^{\prime})\in E^{\mathcal{A}_{2}}_{\downarrow}
iff

•

v,v^{\prime}\in V^{\mathcal{A}_{2}}
and
(v,v^{\prime})\in E^{\mathcal{A}_{2}}
;

•

v=\overrightarrow{m}_{1}+\overleftarrow{n}_{1}+i
for
i\in\mathsf{in}^{\mathcal{B}}
and
(i,v^{\prime})\in E^{\mathcal{A}_{2}}
;

•

v^{\prime}=\overleftarrow{m}_{1}+\overrightarrow{n}_{1}+o
for
o\in\mathsf{out}^{\mathcal{B}}
and
(v,o)\in E^{\mathcal{A}_{2}}
.

Intuitively, the monoidal product of two games simply juxtaposes the two graphs and renumbers the entry and exit positions of the second game. The first example below will be the unit for this operation; the second one is another simple open parity game that reorder the entry and exit positions.

Example II.9
.

(
i
) The
empty game

(0,0)\to(0,0)
is the open parity game given by
((0,0),(0,0),\emptyset,\emptyset,\emptyset,!_{\emptyset})
.

(
ii
) The
swap
game
\sigma^{\overline{m}}_{\overline{n}}=(\overline{m}+\overline{n},\overline{n}+\overline{m},\emptyset,\emptyset,E^{\sigma},!_{\emptyset})
where the sum of pairs represents the pair of component-wise sums and
E^{\sigma}:=\big\{(k,\overrightarrow{n}+k)\mid k\in\left[\overrightarrow{m}\right]\big\}\cup\big\{(\overrightarrow{m}+k,k)\mid k\in\left[\overrightarrow{n}\right]\big\}\cup\big\{(k,\overleftarrow{m}+k)\mid k\in\left[\overleftarrow{n}\right]\big\}\cup\big\{(\overleftarrow{n}+k,k)\mid k\in\left[\overleftarrow{m}\right]\big\}
. For instance,

Up to a suitable notion of syntactic equivalence, it is possible to show that open parity games form a symmetric monoidal category
[
WEAH21
, Theorem 2.10]
. However, since we will only care about a coarser notion of semantic equivalence, we postpone the definition of the category of open parity game to the next subsection.

II-C

Equivalence of open parity games

The main question associated with a given parity game is that of determining the winning positions for each player. We now extend this notion in a compositional way to open parity games, following the work of Watanabe et al. If parity games are positionally determined, the entry and exit positions of open parity games require us to keep track of more information. Plays in an open parity game are defined analogously to plays in their closed counterpart: they are (finite or infinite) sequences of positions that follow edges of the game. Note that, for open parity games, plays that include some exit position
o
are necessarily finite and end with
o
(this is because we have defined exit positions as sink nodes in the graph corresponding to the game). Conversely, a play (finite or infinite) that contains some entry position
i
necessarily starts with
i
(because entry positions are defined to be source nodes in the corresponding graph).

Winning conditions for infinite plays in open parity games are the same as for standard parity games: an infinite play is
winning
for Player
0
(resp.
1
), if it satisfies the parity condition,
i.e.
, if the maximum priority that occurs infinitely often is even (resp. odd). Similarly, finite plays that end at an internal position of an open parity game are winning for the player who does not own the last position. The situation is less clear for finite play that ends at an exit position. How to interpret the outcome of such a play? To answer this question, Watanabe et al move from a purely qualitative (winning or losing) definition to a quantitative one: the denotation of a finite play that ends at an exit position
o
is the pair
(o,k)
where
k
is the highest priority encountered along the play.

Definition II.10
.

Given a play
(v_{i})_{i\in I}
on an open parity game, its
denotation

\{\!|(v_{i})_{i\in I}|\!\}_{\mathcal{A}}
is given by

(o,k)
if
I
is finite, ends on exit position
o
and
k=\max\{\Omega(v_{i})\mid i\in I\}
;
by
\top
if
I
is infinite and
(v_{i})_{i\in I}
is winning for Player
0
;
by
\bot
if
I
is infinite and
(v_{i})_{i\in I}
is winning for Player
1
.

Definition II.11
.

In an open parity game
\mathcal{A}\,:\,\overline{m}\to\overline{n}
, a strategy for Player
0
, or
0
-
strategy
is a function
\sigma\,:\,(\mathsf{in}^{\mathcal{A}}+V)^{*}V_{0}\to V+\mathsf{out}^{\mathcal{A}}
where
(v_{k},\sigma(v_{1}\dots v_{k}))\in E
. In other words, it is a function that chooses a new position adjacent to
v_{k}
for each finite sequence of positions
v_{1}\dots v_{k}
ending in a position that Player
0
controls. Strategies for Player
1
are defined in an analogous way.

For
0
-strategy
\sigma_{0}
and
1
-strategy
\sigma_{1}
,
the play induced by

\sigma_{0}
and
\sigma_{1}
, starting at position
v
, is the sequence
\mathsf{play}_{\sigma_{0},\sigma_{1}}^{v}
of positions given by
v_{1}=v
and
v_{n+1}=\sigma_{0}(v_{1}\dots v_{n})
if
v_{n}\in V_{0}
and
v_{n+1}=\sigma_{1}(v_{1}\dots v_{n})
otherwise.

Definition II.12
.

The
denotation

\{\!|i,\sigma_{0}|\!\}_{\mathcal{A}}
of an entry position
i\in\mathsf{in}^{\mathcal{A}}
and
0
-strategy
\sigma_{0}
in an open parity game
\mathcal{A}\,:\,\overline{m}\to\overline{n}
is
lose
if there is a
1
-strategy
\sigma_{1}
such that
\{\!|\mathsf{play}_{\sigma_{0},\sigma_{1}}^{v}|\!\}_{\mathcal{A}}=\bot
; otherwise
\{\!|i,\sigma_{0}|\!\}_{\mathcal{A}}
is the set

\bigg\{\{\!|\mathsf{play}_{\sigma_{0},\sigma_{1}}^{v}|\!\}_{\mathcal{A}}\,\bigg|\,\sigma_{1}\text{ is a $1$-strategy},\{\!|\mathsf{play}_{\sigma_{0},\sigma_{1}}^{v}|\!\}_{\mathcal{A}}\neq\top\bigg\}

The
semantics
of
\mathcal{A}\,:\,\overline{m}\to\overline{n}
, written
\mathcal{W}_{M}\left(\mathcal{A}\right)
, is the collection:

\begin{gathered}\big\{(T,i)\in\mathcal{P}\left(\mathsf{out}^{\mathcal{A}}\times\mathbb{P}\right)\times\mathsf{in}^{\mathcal{A}}\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\\
\;\,\big|\,\{\!|i,\sigma_{0}|\!\}_{\mathcal{A}}\subseteq T,\{\!|i,\sigma_{0}|\!\}_{\mathcal{A}}\neq\textbf{lose}\text{ for some $0$-strategy }\sigma_{0}\big\}\end{gathered}

Intuitively,
(T,i)
belongs to
\mathcal{W}_{M}\left(\mathcal{A}\right)
, if Player
0
has a strategy such that, for any strategy of Player
1
, the induced play starting at
i
will end in
some
exit positions
o
of
T
, with maximum priority encountered
k
if
(o,k)\in T
. So, in a sense, the smaller
T
is, the more control Player
0
has over the game, and the less influence Player
1
’s strategy has. In particular, if
(\emptyset,i)\in\mathcal{W}_{M}\left(\mathcal{A}\right)
then Player
0
has a winning strategy starting from
i
. Conversely, if
\mathcal{W}_{M}\left(\mathcal{A}\right)
contains no pair
(T,i)
, then Player
1
has a winning strategy starting from
i
. In all intermediate cases, the outcome of the game is not determined in the usual sense, as it will depends on what happens when the play exits
\mathcal{A}
. Crucially, for any open parity game if
\mathcal{A}
has not exit positions, that is, if its codomain is
(0,0)
, then
\mathcal{W}_{M}\left(\mathcal{A}\right)
contains precisely the information about which player wins from which entry position. In this sense, the semantics of open parity games extends the usual notion of winning region of parity games in a faithful way.

Definition II.13
.

We define the following equivalence relation on open parity games:
\mathcal{A}\simeq\mathcal{B}
if the two games
\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}\,:\,m\to n
have the same semantics; we say that
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
are
equivalent
.

Remark II.14
.

It is possible to organise the relations that provide the semantics of open parity games into a traced monoidal category
[
WEAH21
, Section 5]
whose morphisms are certain
monotone
relations, defined as the coKleisli category of a composite comonad based on the work of Grellois and Melliès
[
GM15
]
. This makes
\mathcal{W}_{M}
into a traced symmetric monoidal functor, called the
winning position functor
.

However, we have found computing the composition of these relations to be complicated in practice and often less intuitive than reasoning with strategies directly, at least for the purposes of this paper. For this reason, we only use the semantics to define equivalence of open parity games and use the results of Watanabe et al to show that they form a trace symmetric monoidal category
up to equivalence
, thereby warranting our use of string diagrams in the following section.

There is another difference between our work and that of Watanabe et al: in this paper, we do not use the
Int-construction
, a well-known technique to turn a traced monoidal category into a compact-closed one
[
JSV96
]
. Given our aims, we have found it unnecessary here: from the perspective of open parity games as graphs, we do not need to define a trace operation explicitly, since the graphs we consider admit incoming and outgoing edges both in their domain and codomain, and composition is therefore sufficient to form loops. From the semantic perspective, we can rely on the results of Watanabe et al to show that open games up to equivalence already form a compact-closed category and therefore we have no need for the explicit use of the Int-construction (though we use it implicitly by our appeal to results in that paper).

Theorem II.15
.

Open parity games up to
\simeq
, with the operations of composition (with identities as unit), monoidal product (with the empty game as unit), swap
defined above, form a
symmetric monoidal category, which we call
\mathsf{OPG}_{M}
.

Proof.

The first remark is that the morphisms of
\mathsf{OPG}_{M}
with the operations of composition and monoidal product defined earlier are the same as those of the symmetric monoidal category of the same name in the work of Watanabe et al
[
WEAH21
, Definition 2.11]
. As we have mentioned, the main difference is that they define it using the Int-construction, but it suffices to unpack their definition to realise that our operations on open parity games and theirs are the same (because we build them straight-away using bidirectional composition, while they proceed in two steps, starting from a traced monoidal category of games whose entry positions are all on the left and whose exit position are all on the right, and apply the Int-construction to it).

Secondly, we will need the fact that the semantic mapping
\mathcal{W}_{M}
is a symmetric monoidal functor
[
WEAH21
, Theorem 5.8]
into a certain symmetric monoidal category of monotone relations
[
WEAH21
, Section 4]
, which the authors call
\mathsf{Int}\left(\textbf{FinScottL}_{!_{M}}^{op}\right)
, though we do not need to define it here.
Now, consider four open parity games such that
\mathcal{A}\simeq\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
and
\mathcal{B}\simeq\mathcal{B}^{\prime}
, that is, such that
\mathcal{W}_{M}(\mathcal{A})=\mathcal{W}_{M}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})
and
\mathcal{W}_{M}(\mathcal{B})=\mathcal{W}_{M}(\mathcal{B}^{\prime})
. The functoriality of
\mathcal{W}_{M}
implies that
\mathcal{W}_{M}(\mathcal{A}\,;\,\mathcal{B})=\mathcal{W}_{M}(\mathcal{A})\bm{;}\mathcal{W}_{M}(\mathcal{B})=\mathcal{W}_{M}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})\,;\,\mathcal{W}_{M}(\mathcal{B}^{\prime})=\mathcal{W}_{M}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\,;\,\mathcal{B}^{\prime})
, where the middle operation
;
is the composition in
\mathsf{Int}\left(\textbf{FinScottL}_{!_{M}}^{op}\right)
. From this, we can conclude that
\mathcal{A}\,;\,\mathcal{B}\simeq\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\,;\,\mathcal{B}^{\prime}
or, in other words, that
\simeq
is a congruence for the operation of composition. Moreover, if
\mathcal{W}_{M}\big((\mathcal{A}\,;\,\mathcal{B})\,;\,\mathcal{C}\big)=\big(\mathcal{W}_{M}(\mathcal{A})\bm{;}\mathcal{W}_{M}(\mathcal{B})\big)\bm{;}\mathcal{W}_{M}(\mathcal{C})=\mathcal{W}_{M}(\mathcal{A})\bm{;}\big(\mathcal{W}_{M}(\mathcal{B})\bm{;}\mathcal{W}_{M}(\mathcal{C})\big)=\mathcal{W}_{M}\big(\mathcal{A}\,;\,(\mathcal{B}\,;\,\mathcal{C})\big)
, by associativity of composition in
\mathsf{Int}\left(\textbf{FinScottL}_{!_{M}}^{op}\right)
, so that
(\mathcal{A}\,;\,\mathcal{B})\,;\,\mathcal{C}\simeq\mathcal{A}\,;\,(\mathcal{B}\,;\,\mathcal{C})
, showing that the composition of open parity games up to equivalence is associative.

A similar reasoning, using the fact that
\mathcal{W}_{M}
is
symmetric monoidal shows that
\simeq
is a congruence for the monoidal product,
and that the laws of symmetric monoidal categories hold up to equivalence.
∎

III
A diagrammatic calculus for parity games

III-A

Diagrammatic syntax

Our syntax will be defined as a
prop
, a strict symmetric monoidal category whose objects are all products of some finite set of objects. More specifically, it will be a prop which is freely generated by a given signature, a set of generating objects and morphisms. We will represent the morphisms of this category as
string diagrams
, the natural two-dimensional syntax of symmetric monoidal categories. For a gentle introduction to string diagrams we refer the reader to Selinger’s classic survey
[
Sel11
]
or Piedeleu and Zanasi’s recent text
[
PZ23b
]
. The reader who would like a formal account of the construction of free props from a given signature will find it in the work of Baez, Coya and Rebro on network theory
[
BCR18
, Appendix B]
.

Definition III.1
.

Let
\mathsf{Syn}_{M}
be the two-coloured prop freely generated by the following objects and morphisms:

•

the two generating objects,
\blacktriangleright
(right) and
\blacktriangleleft
(left), whose identities we will depict respectively as the directed wires
and
;

•

the generating morphisms in (

) and (

) below.

Fig. 1:
Axioms of symmetric monoidal categories. The variables
c,c_{1},c_{2},\dots,d_{1},\dots
range over all possible diagrams of the appropriate type (labels of domains and codomains are omitted for legibility). The dotted frames on the first line indicate the order of application of composition and the monoidal product; on the second line they indicate identities when they surround a plain wire, or the unit for the monoidal product when they surround an empty space.

III-B

Semantics of diagrams

We are now ready to define the semantics of our diagram as a symmetric monoidal functor from
\mathsf{Syn}_{M}
to
\mathsf{OPG}_{M}
. Since
\mathsf{Syn}_{M}
is free, we only need to specify how to interpret each of the generating objects and morphisms.

Definition III.2
.

Let
\left\llbracket{\cdot}\right\rrbracket\,:\,\mathsf{Syn}_{M}\to\mathsf{OPG}_{M}
be the symmetric monoidal functor fully specified by

•

\left\llbracket{\blacktriangleright}\right\rrbracket=(1,0)
and
\left\llbracket{\blacktriangleleft}\right\rrbracket=(0,1)
on objects;

•

the mapping given in Fig.
2
on morphisms.

Then, by symmetric monoidal functoriality, the semantics of the (horizontal) composite of two diagrams
c\,:\,u\to v
and
d\,:\,v\to w
is given by
\left\llbracket{c}\right\rrbracket;\left\llbracket{d}\right\rrbracket
, following Definition
II.5
, the semantics of the monoidal product (vertical juxtaposition) of two diagrams
d_{1}\,:\,v_{1}\to w_{1}
and
d_{2}\,:\,v_{2}\to w_{2}
is given by
\left\llbracket{d_{1}}\right\rrbracket\otimes\left\llbracket{d_{2}}\right\rrbracket
, following Definition
II.8
, and the semantics of wire crossings is

\displaystyle=\big(0,1,\{v\},\emptyset,\{(v,\mathtt{r}(1))\},\{v\mapsto 0\}\big)

Fig. 2:
Interpretation of generators as open parity games. Recall that the first two components are the type (domain and codomain) of the corresponding game, the third is the set of internal positions (either empty for the cups and caps, or some arbitrary single node labelled
v
for all the other generators), the fourth is the set of nodes that belong to Player
0
, the fifth is the set of edges, and the last one is the labelling function. Notice that the cup and cap have the same denotation

Now that we have fixed the syntax and semantics of our diagrammatic language, we can check that it is sufficiently expressive to encode arbitrary open parity games. Before reading the proof of the following theorem, we encourage the reader to consult the example in Fig.
3
.

Fig. 3:
Translation of the open parity game in Example
II.4
into a diagram with the same semantics. The framed sub-diagrams encode the positions of the same colour on the left.

Theorem III.3

(Universality)
.

For any open parity game
\mathcal{A}\,:\,m\to n
there exists a diagram
d_{\mathcal{A}}\,:\,\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
such that
\left\llbracket{d_{\mathcal{A}}}\right\rrbracket\simeq\mathcal{A}
.

Proof.

To prove this, we can encode the graph of
\mathcal{A}
directly, as follows: first, for every Player
0
position
v\in V^{\mathcal{A}}
with priority
k
,
m_{v}
incoming edges and
n_{v}
outgoing edges let
d_{v}
be the diagram obtained by sequentially composing
m_{v}-1

-generators, followed by a
k
, and
n_{v}-1

generators, as depicted below:

Then, we can simply juxtapose all
d_{v}
for
v\in V^{\mathcal{A}}
vertically using the monoidal product, obtaining a single diagram with
\sum_{v\in V^{\mathcal{A}}}m_{v}+m
inputs and
\sum_{v\in V^{\mathcal{A}}}n_{v}+n
outputs. We can then use
and
to connect each output that are is no exit positions of
\mathcal{A}
to the corresponding input that is not an entry position, forming the edges of
\mathcal{A}
. These must match exactly, by the handshaking lemma for directed graphs, since
\sum_{v\in V^{\mathcal{A}}}m_{v}=\sum_{v\in V^{\mathcal{A}}}
is the number of internal edges of
\mathcal{A}
.

The diagram we obtain is
d_{\mathcal{A}}
, which satisfies
\left\llbracket{d_{\mathcal{A}}}\right\rrbracket\simeq\mathcal{A}
by construction.
∎

Note that there is another way to prove the previous theorem: from our definition of the semantics of open parity games, it is clear that every game is equivalent to a finite one. We can therefore always construct
d_{\mathcal{A}}
to be a in a simple form that we will later call the
normal form
of diagrams (Definition
IV.3
).

IV
Axiomatisation

This section contains our main technical results: an equational theory which we show is sound and complete for equivalence of open parity games. In other words, we will give a finite set of axioms which correspond to valid semantic equalities (soundness) and which are sufficient to derive any semantic equality between diagrams (completeness).

IV-A

Equational theory

The axioms of Parity Game Algebra (PGA) are given in Fig.
4
to
8
. Let us explain them in more details.

1.

Fig.
4
contains the axioms of
compact-closed categories

[
KL80
]
, a common feature of graphical calculi. These axioms allow us to bend and straighten wires at will, while only keeping track of their direction. Moreover, we include in this group an axiom which allows us to remove a single loop with no entry or exit points. From the perspective of parity games, such diagrams represent inaccessible games, whose outcome is therefore irrelevant.

2.

Fig.
5
contains the axioms of
distributive lattices
. We can think of
as a form of disjunction and
as a form of conjunction. Some of the axioms admit intuitive readings in terms of strategies. For example,
is a counit for
, witnessing the fact that Player
0
would never choose to lose the game immediately, and would always continue on the branch that is not blocked by
instead. The same holds for Player
1
with
and
.

3.

Fig.
6
contains the axioms for the algebraic theory of priorities (also known as the colouring comonad
[
GM15
]
). They guarantee that priorities distribute over
and
, and that they compose sequentially by taking their maximum, a key feature of how they interact in parity games. Finally, since
0
is the minimum of
\mathbb{P}
, it acts as a unit for composition,
i.e.
the identity.

4.

Fig.
7
contains axioms for the distributive law of priorities over lattices: in other words, the priority labels distribute over all four lattice operations (including constants). These equalities are self-evident from the point of view of strategies. The semantics of open games can be formulated explicitly as a the coKleisli category of a certain comonad obtained by composing two comonads via a distributive law
[
WEAH21
]
. These axioms give an equational presentation of this law, though we will not make the connection with distributive laws precise in this paper.

5.

Fig.
8
contains the axiom that encodes the parity condition. It states that, when the loop priority
p
is even, Player
1
has only one non-losing strategy: choosing the first exit and avoiding the loop which would be winning for Player
0
. In this case, Player
0
will have two strategies: passing control to Player
1
or taking the second exit. On the other hand, when
p
is odd, Player
0
has only one non-losing strategy: choosing the second exit, since Player
1
has a winning strategy by taking the loop.

Fig. 8:
Parity axiom

Finally, as mentioned earlier, since
\mathsf{Syn}_{M}
is defined to be a symmetric monoidal category, our diagrams also obey the laws of Fig.
1
. We do not think of these axioms as part of our equational theory, but rather as a form of structural equivalence between diagrams, which we will often use implicitly. When we do use it explicitly, we will denote it by
\equiv
.

We write
\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny PGA}}}{=}}
for the smallest congruence (w.r.t to vertical and horizontal compositions) that includes the axioms of PGA. In practice, diagrammatic reasoning works like a two-dimensional generalisation of standard algebraic reasoning: if we find a sub-diagram that matches one side of an axiom in a larger diagram, we can replace it with the other side of the axiom (the left and right hand side of any axiom have the same type)
[
PZ23b
, Section 2.1]

Theorem IV.1

(Soundness)
.

For any two diagrams
c,d\,:\,v\to w
, if
c\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny PGA}}}{=}}d
then
\left\llbracket{c}\right\rrbracket\simeq\left\llbracket{d}\right\rrbracket
.

Proof.

It suffices to verify that all the axioms of PGA correspond to valid semantic equivalences. We have already given an intuitive account of some of the axioms in the description above; let us cover one example in more detail:

Both diagrams have a single entry position, so their semantics is the set of sets (of denotations of) possible plays starting from
1
that oppose a Player
0
strategy to a Player
1
strategy (Definition
II.12
). Both diagrams correspond to games that only allow finite plays, so the denotation of any play will be a pair of an exit position and a priority (which in this case, will always be zero, since all priorities are zero here).

For the lhs, Player
1
has two strategies: move from the only internal position they control to either of the first two exit positions. Player
0
also has two strategies: move to the internal position controlled by Player
1
or to the last exit position. Playing these strategies against each other and taking the denotation of the induced plays gives:

\mathcal{W}_{M}\left(\left\llbracket{d_{lhs}}\right\rrbracket\right)=\big\{(T,1)\mid\{(1,0),(2,0)\}\subseteq T\text{ or }\{(3,0)\}\subseteq T\big\}

For the rhs, Player
0
has four strategies: two exit choices for each of the two internal positions that they control. Player
1
on the other hand only has two strategies: move to either of the two nodes that Player
0
controls. Putting these together, we also have

\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{M}\left(\left\llbracket{d_{lhs}}\right\rrbracket\right)=\big\{(T,1)\,\mid\;

\displaystyle\{(1,0),(2,0)\}\subseteq T

or

\displaystyle\{(1,0),(3,0)\}\subseteq T

or

\displaystyle\{(2,0),(3,0)\}\subseteq T

or

\displaystyle\{(3,0)\}\subseteq T

\displaystyle\big\}

which is equal to
\mathcal{W}_{M}\left(\left\llbracket{d_{lhs}}\right\rrbracket\right)
.
The soundness of all other axioms can be verified analogously.
∎

Remark IV.2

(Free prop vs free traced prop)
.

We could have presented our syntax as a free
traced
prop instead of a free prop.
However, free traced props are less standard in the literature, and the original work of Watanabe et al prefers a free prop too, perhaps because a compact closed syntax is simpler to use and to present, axiomatically. Another reason to prefer a free prop is that the diagrams one can draw in a compact closed syntax resembles more closely the directed graphs commonly used to represent parity games.

IV-B

Completeness

Our proof of completeness follows a normal form argument, which proceeds in two steps:

1.

First, we explain how to normalise diagrams corresponding to games that do not contain loops,
i.e.
for which there are no non-trivial path from a position to itself.

2.

Then, we normalise arbitrary diagrams, by removing loops, thereby rewriting them to acyclic ones.

IV-B
1
Acyclic case

Formally, we say that a diagram
\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
is
acyclic
if it is composed only of generators from (
1
). As we said, these correspond to particularly simple open games, for which there are no infinite plays.

The following normal form for acyclic diagrams is a generalisation of conjunctive normal form (CNF) for Boolean formulas. The difference is that it includes a layer of
p
. Here, by
layer
(of a certain subset) of generators we mean a diagram composed exclusively of these generators, possibly including identities and wire-crossings.

Definition IV.3
.

Any diagram
d\,:\,\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
is in
normal form
when it factors into a layer of

Theorem IV.4
.

If
c,d\,:\,\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
are two acyclic diagrams in normal form such that
\left\llbracket{c}\right\rrbracket\simeq\left\llbracket{d}\right\rrbracket
, then
c\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny PGA}}}{=}}d
.

Proof.

This proof is the diagrammatic equivalent of showing that any two Boolean formulas in CNF are equal iff they contain the same clauses (
i.e.
that lists of lists up to associativity, commutativity and idempotence are equivalent to sets of sets). The only difference comes from how we deal with the priority labels; but, since they distribute over other generators, the proof is similar.

First, we can always assume that
c
and
d
contain no sub-diagrams of the form

or

by applying co-unitality to rewrite them to an identity wire. Similarly, we can assume that the second layer of
c
and
d
does not contain sub-diagrams of the form

or

By the definition of
\left\llbracket{\cdot}\right\rrbracket
(Fig.
2
), the semantics of acyclic diagrams are open games whose graph do not contain any loops and therefore only allow finite plays. By definition, the first layer of
d
is made of
or
generators. Thus, given some entry
i\in\left[m\right]
of
\left\llbracket{d}\right\rrbracket
, assume we first have
n_{0}
sequentially composed
generators (or a single
if
n_{0}=0
) connected to the
i
-th input in the first layer of
d
. Semantically, each of the possible
n_{0}+1
outputs of these
n_{0}

nodes, corresponds to a strategy of Player
0
, which we call
\sigma_{0}^{k}
for
1\leq k\leq n_{0}+1
.

Now, assume also that, we have
(n^{1}_{j})_{1\leq j\leq n_{0}+1}

nodes (or
if
n^{1}_{j}=0
) connected to each of the
n_{0}+1
outputs of this layer, the outputs of which are each followed by a single priority generator
p
,
p:=p_{k,j}
, for
1\leq k\leq n_{0}
and
1\leq j\leq n^{1}_{k}
. Then, each of these priority generators is connected to an output
o_{k,j}\in\left[n\right]
via
, which defines a possible strategy of Player
1
.

By Definition
II.12
, the denotation of the pair
i,\sigma_{0}^{k}
for
1\leq k\leq n_{0}+1
is

\{\!|i,\sigma_{0}^{k}|\!\}_{\left\llbracket{d}\right\rrbracket}=\{(o_{k,j},p_{k,j})\mid 1\leq j\leq n^{1}_{k}\}

Thus, we see from that any two acyclic diagrams
c,d\,:\,\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}

connected to

in the first layer (or exactly one

or
for each of the outputs of the first layer, each followed by the same priority for each output to which they are connected via
. Hence

and

can only differ in the following three ways:

they have a different number of

the tree of

where the first equality uses the fact that acyclic diagrams can be merged,

For 3) we can use co-associativity and co-commutativity of

(resp.
) which form a tree (

Theorem IV.5

(Acyclic completeness)
.

For any two acyclic diagrams
c,d\,:\,\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
, if
\left\llbracket{c}\right\rrbracket\simeq\left\llbracket{d}\right\rrbracket
then
c\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny PGA}}}{=}}d
.

Proof.

We proceed using a standard normalisation argument: given an acyclic diagram
d
, we give a procedure to rewrite it to a diagram
d^{\prime}
in normal form, using only the axioms of PGA, so that
d=d^{\prime}
. Since normal forms uniquely represent each class of diagrams up to semantic equivalence (Theorem
IV.4
), any two acyclic diagrams that denote the same open parity game will thus be equal to the same normal form, and therefore equal to each other, by transitivity of equality.

The main idea of the normalisation argument is to use the distributivity of
p
over
,
, and
,
in order to push all of the priority nodes to the right of these four generators, combining them using the maximum axiom when necessary. Then we can use the distributive lattice axioms to reorganise
,
, and
,
in the order needed. We obtain some extra
,
that we can push past the
p
using the distributivity of the latter over the former, until we are done. While this is an easy proof by structural induction, which is very close to the proof that any Boolean formula is equivalent to one in CNF, we could not find a reference, so we include it in Appendix,
cf.
Lemma
.2
.
∎

IV-B
2
General case

For games that may contain cycles (and therefore infinite plays) the key idea is that all such cycles can be removed. Indeed, intuitively, this is the case in the semantics: if a cycle is a winning play for one of the players, we should be able to rewrite it to a
or
. This is precisely what the parity axiom allows us to do.

Theorem IV.6

(Completeness of PGA)
.

For any two diagrams
c,d\,:\,v\to w
, if
\left\llbracket{c}\right\rrbracket\simeq\left\llbracket{d}\right\rrbracket
then
c\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny PGA}}}{=}}d
.

Proof.

First, without loss of generality, we can restrict ourselves to diagrams
\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
, since the category is compact closed,
cf.
Lemma
.3
in Appendix.

Now assume that we have two diagrams
c,d\,:\,\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
such that
\left\llbracket{c}\right\rrbracket\simeq\left\llbracket{d}\right\rrbracket
. The key idea is that if we can show that
c
and
d
are equal to
acyclic
diagrams, the theorem follows from acyclic completeness (Theorem
IV.5
).

We are thus going to show that any diagram
\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
is equal to an acyclic one. Reasoning by induction, it is enough to show that we can remove a single loop,
i.e.
, that given an acyclic diagram
b\,:\,\blacktriangleright^{1+m}\to\blacktriangleright^{1+n}
, the diagram below is provably equal to an acyclic diagram:

(3)

We now reason by induction on the number of generators in
b
. For the base case, if
b
is composed of zero generators, it consists exclusively of identities and symmetries, and thus
\mathsf{Tr}^{1}_{m,n}(b)
can be proved equal to an acyclic diagram using only the axioms of compact closed categories (Fig.
4
). This is a standard fact about the free compact closed category on some generating objects, whose proof can be found in
[
Abr05
]
. For the inductive case, assume that, for any acyclic diagram
b
with up to
k
generators,
\mathsf{Tr}^{1}_{m,n}(b)
is equal to an acyclic diagram. We now want to show that this holds for
b
with
k+1
generators.

Since
b
is acyclic, it is provably equal to one in normal form, by Theorem
IV.5
. This means that there exists a diagram
b^{\prime}
and some priority
p
such that

\displaystyle\hbox to46.55pt{\vbox to25.8pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 23.54808pt\lower-8.2pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \hbox to0.0pt{
{

Note that we have strictly decreased the number of generators in
b
in both cases, so we can apply the induction hypothesis to rewrite the resulting diagram into an acyclic one.
∎

As we claimed in the introduction, the completeness of PGA allows us to solve parity games using equational reasoning. First, notice that any parity game
(V,V_{0},E,\Omega)
can be seen as an
open
parity game
\mathcal{A}\,:\,|V|\to 0
with all positions as entry positions (and no exits); using the universality of our syntax, we can encode
\mathcal{A}
as a diagram
d_{\mathcal{A}}\,:\,|V|\to 0
. Second, any diagram in normal form with no outputs is equal to a monoidal product of
and
, indicating which entry positions are winning for each player. Hence, normalising
d_{\mathcal{A}}
solves the parity game with which we started. We refer the reader to Fig.
9
-
10
for a worked example.

V
An alternative symbolic syntax

In this section, we present a syntax which is equivalent to the diagrammatic language of this paper. This kind of correspondence of calculi with fixpoint with string diagrams for traced monoidal categories is now standard and was first proposed by Hasegawa
[
Has12
]
. We sketch it here to show that it is also a viable approach to an algebraic treatment of (open) parity games—one which might be more immediately amenable to computer implementation, even if the connection to parity games is less intuitive than the graphical presentation.

Syntax

We define
game-expressions
inductively with the following grammar:

t::=x\mid\underline{k}\left(t\right)\mid{t}\lor{t}\mid{t}\land{t}\mid\bot\mid\top\mid\mu{x}.{t}

where
x
ranges over some countably infinite set of variables and
k\in\mathbb{P}
. We write
n\vdash t
for a game expression with
n\in\mathbb{N}
free variables
x_{1},\dots,x_{n}
. We keep track of the ordering of the free variables to facilitate the diagrammatic interpretation of expressions below, where they become output wires (and are therefore ordered). The typing rules for the judgment
n\vdash t
are the usual ones for algebraic theories, with the addition of the following fixpoint rule: from
n+1\vdash t
we can derive
n\vdash\mu{x_{n+1}}.{t}
. Of course, we consider expressions up to alpha-equivalence of bound variables.

A game expression is intended to encode an open parity game
with a single entry position
. Intuitively, free variables correspond to exit positions,
{s}\lor{t}
corresponds to a Player
0
choice between positions
s
and
t
,
{s}\land{t}
to a Player
1
choice between positions
s
and
t
,
\bot
to a loss for Player
0
,
\top
to a win for Player
0
,
\underline{k}\left(t\right)
to a node with in-and out-degree one, and priority
k\in\mathbb{P}
, and
\mu{x}.{t}
to a loop joining the exit position
x
to the start position of
t
.

Example V.1
.

The open parity game

2
4
1
3

corresponds to the expression with one free variable

\mu y_{4}.\mu y_{1}.\underline{4}\left(\underline{1}\left(y_{1}\land x_{1}\right)\right)\lor\mu y_{3}.\underline{3}\left(\underline{2}\left(y_{4}\land\underline{1}\left(y_{1}\land x_{1}\right)\land y_{3}\right)\right)

Semantics

We interpret game-expressions inductively, as diagrams. As mentioned above, a similar interpretation of calculi with fixpoint into traced monoidal categories can be found in the original work of Hasegawa
[
Has12
]
. The main idea is that a game-expression
t
with
n
free variables is translated into a diagram
\llparenthesis{\,n\vdash t\,}\rrparenthesis\,:\,\blacktriangleright\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
.

\displaystyle\llparenthesis{\,n\vdash x_{k}\,}\rrparenthesis

To obtain an interpretation in terms of open parity games, we simply apply
\left\llbracket{\cdot}\right\rrbracket
to the resulting diagrams (or, by completeness of PGA, consider two expressions semantically equal when their diagrammatic translations are equal up to
\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny PGA}}}{=}}\;
).

Axioms

With the interpretation above, up to equality of diagrams, it is easy to see that
{}\lor{},{}\land{},\bot,\top
form a distributive lattice (
B
), that
\underline{k}\left(\cdot\right)
distributes over the lattice operations (
D
), satisfies
\underline{k^{\prime}}\left(\underline{k}\left(x\right)\right)\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny C3}}}{=}}\underline{\max{(k,k^{\prime})}}\left(x\right)
,
\underline{0}\left(x\right)\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny C4}}}{=}}x
,
and the following parity condition:

\mu{y}.{\big({x_{0}}\lor{({x_{1}}\land{\underline{k}\left(y\right)})}\big)}\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny E}}}{=}}\begin{cases}{x_{0}}\lor{x_{1}}&\text{if $k$ is even};\\
x_{0}&\text{if $k$ is odd}.\end{cases}

Since a lot of the symbolic axioms have a diagrammatic counterpart, we keep the axioms labels consistent with those of Fig.
5
-
8
where possible.

We also need axioms that allow us to swap fixpoints,
\mu{x}.{\mu{y}.{t}}\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny F1}}}{=}}\mu{y}.{\mu{x}.{t}}
, and to remove a fixpoint
\mu{x}.{t}
when
x
does not occur free in
t
: in this case
\mu{x}.{t}\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny F2}}}{=}}t
. Interestingly, in the presence of the other axioms, the usual fixpoint equation
\mu{x}.{t}=t[\mu{x}.{t}/x]
, where
t[u/x]
denotes the substitution of
u
for all occurrences of the variable
x
in
t
, is derivable. This is because, as in the diagrammatic syntax, fixpoints can be removed, and any expression is equal to one in CNF, or rather, a suitable generalisation thereof that includes priorities (the symbolic counterpart of Definition
IV.3
).

Finally, using the results of this paper, or symbolic translations of the same proofs, it would not be difficult to show that these axioms are sound and complete for the intended interpretation. As before, we can use the equational theory to solve parity games. Rather than a tedious reproduction of the diagrammatic proofs, we illustrate the idea with the following symbolic derivation.

Example V.2
.

Coming back to Example
V.1
, we can close the only exit position of the game by setting the free variable
x_{1}
to
\top
in the corresponding game-expression. We obtain,

\displaystyle\mu y_{4}.\mu y_{1}.\underline{4}\left(\underline{1}\left(y_{1}\land\top\right)\right)\lor\mu y_{3}.\underline{3}\left(\underline{2}\left(y_{4}\land\underline{1}\left(y_{1}\land\top\right)\land y_{3}\right)\right)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny B}}}{=}}\mu y_{4}.\mu y_{1}.\underline{4}\left(\underline{1}\left(y_{1}\right)\right)\lor\mu y_{3}.\underline{3}\left(\underline{2}\left(y_{4}\land\underline{1}\left(y_{1}\right)\land y_{3}\right)\right)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny C3}}}{=}}\mu y_{4}.\mu y_{1}.\underline{4}\left(\underline{1}\left(y_{1}\right)\right)\lor\mu y_{3}.\underline{3}\left(y_{4}\land\underline{1}\left(y_{1}\right)\land y_{3}\right)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny C3}}}{=}}\mu y_{4}.\mu y_{1}.\underline{4}\left(y_{1}\right)\lor\mu y_{3}.\underline{3}\left(y_{4}\land\underline{1}\left(y_{1}\right)\land y_{3}\right)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny B}}}{=}}\mu y_{4}.\mu y_{1}.\underline{4}\left(y_{1}\right)\lor\mu y_{3}.\bot\lor\underline{3}\left(y_{4}\land\underline{1}\left(y_{1}\right)\land y_{3}\right)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny D}}}{=}}\mu y_{4}.\mu y_{1}.\underline{4}\left(y_{1}\right)\lor\mu y_{3}.\bot\lor\big(\underline{3}\left(y_{4}\land\underline{1}\left(y_{1}\right)\right)\land\underline{3}\left(y_{3}\right)\big)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny E}}}{=}}\mu y_{4}.\mu y_{1}.\underline{4}\left(y_{1}\right)\lor\bot\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny B}}}{=}}\mu y_{4}.\mu y_{1}.\bot\lor(\top\land\underline{4}\left(y_{1}\right))

\displaystyle\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny E}}}{=}}\mu y_{4}.\bot\lor\top\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny B}}}{=}}\mu y_{4}.\top\mathrel{\overset{\makebox[0.0pt]{\mbox{\tiny F2}}}{=}}\top

We have thereby proved again that Player
0
wins from the top right position of the corresponding parity game, as the last diagram in Fig.
10
had already shown.

VI
Discussion and Further Work

We have presented a sound and complete calculus in which parity games can be encoded and solved using equational reasoning—this opens up promising avenues of research.

From the complexity-theoretic perspective, our normalisation procedure requires space exponential in the size of the original diagram/game (in the same way that obtaining a CNF formula equivalent to a given Boolean formula may require exponential space). However, this is not necessarily the case on restricted classes of diagrams. It would be useful to identify sub-categories of diagrams for which solutions are tractable. Perhaps existing work on compositional tractability of parity games for some graph operations
[
DKT16
]
can point us in the right direction.
Moreover, the local flavour of reasoning using equational axioms appears most closely related to strategy improvement algorithms for solving parity games
[
VJ00
]
. Making the potential connection precise is an interesting direction of research.

Finally, it seems possible to extend the present work to alternating parity
automata
, by incorporating the additional structure found in the work of Piedeleu and Zanasi on automata
[
PZ23a
]
and adding observable actions/transitions to open parity games. Indeed, their work shares a lot of the algebraic structure found in open parity games: both diagrammatic calculi are compact closed, with a distributive lattice on each object, so combining them certainly appears possible. Semantically, in order to bridge the two pieces of work, we would require the denotation of parity automata to keep track of the actions performed by the automaton for each possible winning run (for Player
0
) starting from each entry position. Excitingly, this would also open up the way to a diagrammatic treatment of the modal
\mu
-calculus.

The first result about acyclic diagrams is that we can co-copy and co-delete them at will—this gives us a diagrammatic analogue of substitution in a traditional symbolic syntax.

Lemma .1
.

For any acyclic diagram

the following equalities are derivable:

∎

The proof of the following lemma describes the normalisation procedure for acyclic diagrams.

Lemma .2
.

Every acyclic diagram
d\,:\,\blacktriangleright^{m}\to\blacktriangleright^{n}
is equal to one in normal form.

is in normal form, by assumption.

∎

The following lemma implies that, without loss of generality, we need only consider to left-to-right diagrams for our completeness proof.

Lemma .3
.

There are natural bijections between the sets
\mathsf{Syn}_{M}(v_{1}\!\blacktriangleleft\!v_{2},w)
and
\mathsf{Syn}_{M}(v_{1}v_{2},w\!\blacktriangleright)
, and between
\mathsf{Syn}_{M}(v,w_{1}\!\blacktriangleleft\!w_{2})
and
\mathsf{Syn}_{M}(v\!\blacktriangleright,w_{1}w_{2})
,
i.e.
between sets of string diagrams of the form

v_{1}
w
v_{2}
d

and

v_{1}
w
v_{2}
d

w_{1}
v
w_{2}
d

and

w_{1}
v
w_{2}
d

where
v,w,v_{i},w_{i}
are words over
\{\blacktriangleright,\blacktriangleleft\}
.

Proof.

The lemma holds in any compact closed category and relies on the ability to bend wires using
and
. Explicitly, given a diagram of the first form, we can obtain one of the second form as follows:

(5)

The inverse mapping is given by the same wiring with the opposite direction. That they are inverse transformations follows immediately from the defining axioms of compact closed categories (A1-A2). The other bijection is constructed analogously.
∎

Intuitively, Lemma
.3
tells us that we can always bend incoming wires to the left and outgoing wires to the right before applying some equations, and recover the original orientation of the wires by bending them into their original place later.
